metadata.narrative: Design a cross-platform anti-cheat system for a competitive first-person shooter video game that could potentially handle up to 1 million concurrent users across multiple game sessions. Requirements: It should have a true positive detection rate of over 98% and a very low false negative detection rate of less than 2%. It should also be lightweight and shouldn't add much overhead to each of the game's builds. Provide a high-level architecture diagram, an outline of your plan, detection pipeline description, cost estimates using cloud/infra prices available currently (July 2025), and a reproducible test methodology. Any non-obvious fact should be followed by a proper source, and/or a inline URL.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A cross-platform anti-cheat system serving roughly 1 million concurrent players across many simultaneous FPS matches should be organized as five cooperating layers so that no single client build carries excessive overhead.

The first layer is a thin client agent watching for known cheat-process signatures that forwards compact telemetry, such as input timing and aim deltas, rather than raw video, mirroring Riot Vanguard's strategy of modeling mouse acceleration and impulse features to flag aimbot behavior.

The second layer is the authoritative game server, which never trusts client-reported hits and instead keeps its own per-frame physics snapshot and re-raycasts each timestamped shot against stored player positions, the reconciliation and lag-compensation pattern documented in FPS netcode design.
That server state is further hardened with encryption, packet checksums, and signature checking on all synchronized position data.

The third layer is a real-time telemetry bus ingesting per-match events for scoring, the fourth is an ML inference tier combining statistical behavioral features with an optional vision classifier, and the fifth is a human-review and enforcement queue.

The detection pipeline should use three escalating tiers, following the model Riot's anti-cheat lead described publicly: hard signature detection of known cheat binaries triggers instant ejection at high confidence, technical-action detection watches for illegitimate memory or API calls, and behavioral detection scores per-match statistics like aim-duration ratio, effective-targeting ratio, and scoped-kill ratio for review.

The academic VADNet model operationalizes exactly these ratios alongside a convolutional backbone and feature-pyramid neck to classify cheating from match video, reporting precision, recall, and F1 on a held-out test set.

Valve's VACnet shows this at production scale: a Naive Bayes "trust score" sorts suspected cheaters into separate matchmaking pools, then a deep model trained on human "Overwatch" review convictions runs across roughly 3,500 processors against about 150,000 daily matches, lifting conviction accuracy from a 15–30% human baseline to 80–95%.
Valve has described the underlying hardware as a 1,700-CPU farm with headroom to double, an independent scale reference consistent with that processor count.

Batching confirmed detections into periodic wave bans rather than instant bans deliberately slows a cheat developer's detect-evade-detect cycle and prevents sellers from claiming a tool is fully undetectable, why it remains industry standard practice.
Activision's Ricochet system layers in shadow bans that quietly pool flagged accounts together pending manual review, a state players can sometimes infer from abnormal queue times or ping spikes.

On the always-on kernel-driver question, the design should default to a non-kernel approach for cross-platform lightness: Valve's VAC issues periodic client-integrity challenges and scans process memory on demand rather than installing a persistent driver, whereas Riot's Vanguard and Epic's Easy Anti-Cheat run kernel-level drivers for deeper visibility.
Vanguard's driver, named vgk.sys, loads at Windows boot and runs at Ring 0 with elevated admin privileges even when the game is closed.

That always-on privilege has drawn documented privacy and security objections, including comparisons to rootkit behavior and precedent of a similar anti-cheat driver being exploited as an attack vector in Genshin Impact.

Given the 98% true-positive and under-2% false-negative targets, a hybrid is recommended: non-kernel, server-authoritative plus behavioral/vision detection for all platforms by default, with an optional opt-in kernel module reserved for PC ranked competitive queues.

For infrastructure sized to 1 million concurrent users, telemetry ingestion on a managed stream such as AWS Kinesis costs $0.015 per shard-hour plus $0.025 per million PUT payload units, with volume discounts up to 65% at scale.
Match-session compute can run on AWS GameLift's managed EC2 fleets with FlexMatch matchmaking and autoscaling policies that add or remove capacity against idle-instance thresholds across regions.

A reserved r5.2xlarge-class instance runs near $250 per month versus roughly $84 per month for a comparable dedicated 6-core/64GB box, illustrating the premium for managed elasticity, while lighter matchmaking or API services can run on general-purpose instances like t3.medium at $0.0416 per hour on demand.

The behavioral-model inference tier is the dominant ML cost driver; consolidating many model variants onto SageMaker multi-model endpoints on ml.g5.2xlarge instances at $1.52 per instance-hour can cut a naive per-model deployment bill of $218,880 per month down to about $54,720 per month, a 75% reduction, for a hundred-model footprint.

Supporting Kubernetes-orchestrated microservices should run on Spot or Reserved nodes, saving up to roughly 85% versus on-demand pricing, consolidated into as few clusters as possible to avoid duplicated control-plane costs.

Requirements-driven autoscaling can further outperform Kubernetes' default Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, using at least 50% less CPU, 87% less memory, and 90% fewer replicas while still meeting service-level objectives.

Perimeter protection is largely free via AWS Shield Standard, blocking about 96% of common network-layer floods automatically, though Shield Advanced with 24/7 incident response and application-layer WAF rules starts at $3,000 per month, justified for a high-value competitive title.
Overall monthly infrastructure spend at 1 million CCU likely lands in the low-to-mid six figures, dominated by compute-fleet and inference tiers rather than telemetry ingestion.

For reproducible testing, report standard confusion-matrix metrics, where precision equals TP/(TP+FP), recall equals TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is their harmonic mean, evaluated on a held-out labeled dataset split into training, validation, and test partitions the same way the VADNet study organized its image corpus.

To hit a greater-than-98% true-positive rate with a less-than-2% false-negative rate, treat each detector release as a formal hypothesis test with explicit alpha and beta thresholds, where alpha is the false-positive (Type I) rate and beta is the false-negative (Type II) rate whose complement, 1−beta, is statistical power.

Because convention sets alpha near 5% and beta near 20%, meeting a 2% false-negative target requires tightening beta well below that default and validating it against a large fixed sample before deployment.

A concrete protocol: freeze a labeled benchmark of known-cheat and known-clean matches using ground truth from prior human review, run the candidate model to log the full confusion matrix, compute precision, recall, and F1 with bootstrapped confidence intervals, then shadow-deploy for one full ban-wave cycle without enforcing action while comparing flags against the existing human-reviewed conviction-rate baseline.
Only promote the model to live wave-ban enforcement once it clears both thresholds on the frozen benchmark and the live shadow period, re-validating quarterly as cheat techniques evolve.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

A cross-platform anti-cheat system capable of serving roughly 1 million concurrent players across many simultaneous FPS matches should be organized as five cooperating layers so that no single client build carries excessive overhead.
The first layer is a thin client agent that watches for known cheat-process signatures and forwards compact telemetry, such as input timing and aim deltas, rather than raw video, mirroring Riot Vanguard's strategy of modeling mouse acceleration and impulse features to flag aimbot behavior instead of shipping heavy client logic. [shard_00445_76202]
The second layer is the authoritative game server, which never trusts client-reported hits and instead keeps its own per-frame physics snapshot and re-raycasts each timestamped shot against stored player positions, the same reconciliation and lag-compensation pattern documented in FPS netcode design. [shard_02446_19046]
That server state is further hardened with encryption, packet checksums, and signature checking on all synchronized position data. [shard_00483_16453]
The third layer is a real-time telemetry bus that ingests per-match events for scoring, the fourth is an ML inference tier combining statistical behavioral features with an optional vision classifier, and the fifth is a human-review and enforcement queue.

The detection pipeline itself should use three escalating tiers, following the model Riot's anti-cheat lead described publicly: hard signature detection of known cheat binaries triggers instant ejection at high confidence, technical-action detection watches for illegitimate memory or API calls, and behavioral detection scores per-match statistics like aim-duration ratio, effective-targeting ratio, and scoped-kill ratio for manual review. [shard_00445_76202] [shard_02021_23222]
The academic VADNet model operationalizes exactly these ratios alongside a convolutional backbone and feature-pyramid neck to classify cheating from match video, reporting precision, recall, and F1 on a held-out 640×640 image test set. [shard_02021_23222]
Valve's VACnet shows this approach at production scale: a Naive Bayes "trust score" first sorts suspected cheaters into separate matchmaking pools, then a deep model trained on human "Overwatch" review convictions runs across roughly 3,500 processors against about 150,000 daily matches, lifting conviction accuracy from a 15–30% human baseline to 80–95%. [shard_02131_30140]
Valve has described the underlying hardware as a 1,700-CPU farm with headroom to double, an independent scale reference consistent with the processor count above. [shard_04518_37236]
For enforcement, batching confirmed detections into periodic wave bans rather than instant bans deliberately slows a cheat developer's detect-evade-detect cycle and prevents sellers from claiming a tool is fully undetectable, which is why it remains industry standard practice. [shard_01890_45954]
Activision's Ricochet system layers in shadow bans that quietly pool flagged accounts together pending manual review, a state players can sometimes infer from abnormal queue times or ping spikes. [shard_02875_39918]

On the always-on kernel-driver question, the design should default to a non-kernel approach for cross-platform lightness: Valve's VAC issues periodic client-integrity challenges and scans process memory on demand rather than installing a persistent driver, whereas Riot's Vanguard and Epic's Easy Anti-Cheat run kernel-level drivers for deeper visibility. [shard_01832_35224]
Vanguard's driver, named vgk.sys, loads at Windows boot and runs at Ring 0 with elevated admin privileges even when the game is closed. [shard_00474_49659]
That always-on privilege has drawn documented privacy and security objections, including comparisons to rootkit behavior and precedent of a similar anti-cheat driver being exploited as an attack vector in Genshin Impact. [shard_00330_58108]
Given the 98% true-positive and under-2% false-negative targets, a hybrid is recommended: non-kernel, server-authoritative plus behavioral/vision detection for all platforms by default, with an optional opt-in kernel module reserved for PC ranked competitive queues.

For infrastructure sized to 1 million concurrent users, telemetry ingestion on a managed stream such as AWS Kinesis costs $0.015 per shard-hour plus $0.025 per million PUT payload units, with volume discounts of up to 65% at scale. [shard_06482_2120]
Match-session compute can run on AWS GameLift's managed EC2 fleets with FlexMatch matchmaking and autoscaling policies that add or remove capacity against idle-instance thresholds across regions. [shard_02950_71551] [shard_06273_83473]
A reserved r5.2xlarge-class instance runs near $250 per month versus roughly $84 per month for a comparable dedicated 6-core/64GB box, illustrating the premium paid for managed elasticity, while lighter-weight matchmaking or API services can run on general-purpose instances like t3.medium at $0.0416 per hour on demand. [shard_04728_864] [shard_03217_22212]
The behavioral-model inference tier is the dominant ML cost driver; consolidating many model variants onto SageMaker multi-model endpoints on ml.g5.2xlarge instances at $1.52 per instance-hour can cut a naive per-model deployment bill of $218,880 per month down to about $54,720 per month, a 75% reduction, for a hundred-model footprint. [shard_05013_76047]
Supporting Kubernetes-orchestrated microservices should run on Spot or Reserved nodes, saving up to roughly 85% versus on-demand pricing, consolidated into as few clusters as possible to avoid duplicated control-plane costs. [shard_03245_60946]
Requirements-driven autoscaling can further outperform Kubernetes' default Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, using at least 50% less CPU, 87% less memory, and 90% fewer replicas while still meeting service-level objectives. [shard_00926_2099]
Perimeter protection is largely free via AWS Shield Standard, which blocks about 96% of common network-layer floods automatically, though Shield Advanced with 24/7 incident-response support and application-layer WAF rules starts at $3,000 per month, a justified expense for a high-value competitive title. [shard_06100_65263]
Taken together, streaming, compute fleets, ML inference, orchestration, and DDoS protection put rough monthly infrastructure spend at 1 million CCU in the low-to-mid six figures, dominated by the compute-fleet and inference tiers rather than telemetry ingestion.

For reproducible testing, report the standard confusion-matrix metrics, where precision equals TP/(TP+FP), recall equals TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is their harmonic mean, evaluated on a held-out labeled dataset split into training, validation, and test partitions the same way the VADNet study organized its image corpus. [shard_00729_11639] [shard_02021_23222]
To actually hit a greater-than-98% true-positive rate with a less-than-2% false-negative rate, treat each detector release as a formal hypothesis test with explicit alpha and beta thresholds, where alpha is the false-positive (Type I) rate and beta is the false-negative (Type II) rate whose complement, 1−beta, is statistical power. [shard_01169_63326]
Because conventional practice sets alpha near 5% and beta near 20%, meeting a 2% false-negative target requires deliberately tightening beta well below that default and validating the tightened threshold against a large fixed sample before deployment. [shard_01169_63326]
A concrete reproducible protocol is: freeze a labeled benchmark of known-cheat and known-clean matches using ground truth from prior human review, run the candidate model to log the full confusion matrix, compute precision, recall, and F1 with bootstrapped confidence intervals, then shadow-deploy the model for one full ban-wave cycle without enforcing action while comparing its flags against the existing human-reviewed conviction-rate baseline. [shard_02131_30140] [shard_00729_11639]
Only promote the model to live wave-ban enforcement once it clears the 98%/2% thresholds on both the frozen benchmark and the live shadow period, and re-validate the thresholds quarterly as cheat techniques evolve. [shard_01890_45954]

answer.text: A cross-platform anti-cheat system serving roughly 1 million concurrent players across many simultaneous FPS matches should be organized as five cooperating layers so that no single client build carries excessive overhead.

The second layer is the authoritative game server, which never trusts client-reported hits and instead keeps its own per-frame physics snapshot and re-raycasts each timestamped shot against stored player positions, the reconciliation and lag-compensation pattern documented in FPS netcode design.
That server state is further hardened with encryption, packet checksums, and signature checking on all synchronized position data.

The third layer is a real-time telemetry bus ingesting per-match events for scoring, the fourth is an ML inference tier combining statistical behavioral features with an optional vision classifier, and the fifth is a human-review and enforcement queue.

The detection pipeline should use three escalating tiers, following the model Riot's anti-cheat lead described publicly: hard signature detection of known cheat binaries triggers instant ejection at high confidence, technical-action detection watches for illegitimate memory or API calls, and behavioral detection scores per-match statistics like aim-duration ratio, effective-targeting ratio, and scoped-kill ratio for review.
